newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian in another assisted suicide case.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian in another assisted suicide case.

text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian's attorney said Wednesday he had been retained by the family of a 63-year-old Colorado woman suffering from multiple sclerosis in another apparent assisted suicide case.

Attorney Geoffrey Fieger said in a statement the woman, Delouise Bacher, was last known to be at the Quality Inn in Romulus, a Detroit suburb. Fieger did not say if the woman had died, and could not be directly reached for comment.
A spokesman for the Romulus police department said police had responded to a report of a body found at the Quality Inn on Wednesday morning. Police said the identify was not immediately available.
In his statement, Fieger said Bacher, of Arvada, Colorado, suffered from an "extremely progressive" form of multiple sclerosis that had turned her into a quadriplegic.
Fieger said Bacher's family asked him to protect them against attempts by Michigan government officials to invade their privacy.
Since March, five bodies have turned up in local motel rooms with notes referring authorities to Fieger. Fieger has refused to say if Kevorkian was involved in the deaths.
Kevorkian, a retired pathologist, has not admitted to helping someone die since last November. He has publicly acknowledged being present at 45 deaths since 1990.

Kevorkian has been acquited three times on assisted suicide charges. Kevorkian, along with long-time ally Janet Good, were scheduled to go on trial next month in Ionia, Michigan, on assisted suicide and other charges.
But on Wednesday Ionia County Prosecutor Raymond Voet said he was dropping the charges against Good, 73, who says she suffers from terminal pancreatic cancer.

Voet filed motions in Ionia County Circuit Court asking that Good be granted immunity and testify "as soon as possible" via deposition. Those issues will be heard by Circuit Judge Charles Miel at a May 16 hearing.
In February, Voet's request that Kevorkian and Good be tried separately was denied. Voet said the defence had refused his request to be given Good's medical documentation.
"Of course it is unlcear how sick Ms. Good really is," Voet said in a statement explaining Wednesday's motions.
Voet said he "could not discount the possibility that Ms. Good's medical condition was purposely being concealed so she could die in court as a martyr."
Kevorkian and Good were charged in connection with the August 30, 1996, death of Loretta Peabody, a multiple sclerosis victim, at her Ionia home.
